title: Phase-aware upgrade orchestrator for dedicated GPU pools
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: Upgrades to Dedicated GPU pools can cause transient capacity holes when individual nodes are drained for kernel patches or runtime changes. Current drain+scale handoffs are ad-hoc per-pool and depend on manual cadence, which increases risk of throttled requests and degraded tail latency during coordinated upgrades.

Goal: Build a phase-aware orchestrator that coordinates GPU pool draining, autoscaler handshakes, and staged traffic gating so we can roll out runtime and LTS changes across Dedicated fleets with predictable capacity impact and automated rollback triggers. The controller should support: version channels (LTS/stable/canary), explicit phase definitions (prepare, drain, verify, cutover), capacity budgeting, and per-customer routing policies for reserved pools.

Non-goals: This ticket does not implement cross-region routing fallback or full console UI. It focuses on the orchestration primitives and API consumed by higher-level rollout services and the autoscaler integration.
acceptance_criteria: Controller exposes an API to create an upgrade plan with phases and budgeted eviction limits
Autoscaler exposes a handshake endpoint and honors drain window tokens issued by the controller
During a staged rollout test, token drop rate and 99th percentile latency do not regress beyond predefined SLOs for more than 5 minutes
Controller can abort and automatically initiate reverse-evacuation (rebalance) if cluster admission rates drop or error budget thresholds hit
End-to-end integration test covering canary->staged->cutover transitions runs in CI and is reliable under synthetic load
implementation_notes:
Architecture: new 'upgrade-orchestrator' service (Kubernetes deployment) will hold plans and phase state. It emits per-gpu-pool tokens that the 'pool-agent' uses to gate node cordons. Autoscaler will be extended with a lightweight handshake endpoint: /v1/scale-handshake that accepts token metadata and responds with scale actions (scale-up/hold/scale-down).

Drain strategy: adopt a low-churn eviction algorithm that staggers pod reseating across availability zones and respects pinned workloads (dedicated capacity commitments). Use soft-drain first (prevent new allocations), then progressive cordon+evict with backoff.

Metrics & telemetry: add plan-level metrics (plan_id, phase, remaining_budget) and per-pool budget consumption. Emit events to Console rollouts dashboard. Integrations: link to incident-runbook and SLO dashboard in monitoring.

Trade-offs considered: immediate full-evacuation is fastest but risks SLO violations; slow progressive drains minimize risk but prolong exposure. We choose phase durations with dynamic adaptation based on real-time admission and token consumption metrics.
risks: Incorrect budget estimation can starve normal traffic or delay rollouts
Autoscaler handshake bugs could cause oscillation between scaling and draining
Pinned customer workloads may block eviction if not properly discovered
Complexity of multi-tenant reserved pools increases coordination surface
rollout_plan: 1) Prototype controller + local pool-agent integration in dev; 2) Run closed-loop integration tests against synthetic dedicated clusters; 3) Canary a single small reserved pool with non-critical traffic; 4) Observe for two full maintenance windows and validate SLOs; 5) Expand to staged batches by channel (canary->stable->lts).
testing_plan:
- Unit tests for controller state machine
- Integration test that simulates autoscaler handshake and ensures tokens prevent scale-down during drain
- Load test: synthetic request generator to validate latency and admission under drain conditions
- Chaos test: randomly kill pool-agent processes during a staged cutoff to ensure controller recovers
